articles.abstract: Negotiation often involves a recurring tension between self-interest and social preferences such as fairness, trust, honesty, and reciprocity. A central debate concerns which motive, self-interest or social preferences, constitutes the automatic default and which requires cognitive control to be expressed. Understanding these automatic processes is important because negotiations often tax cognitive resources, increasing reliance on automatic responses. Yet, the evidence remains contradictory: in some contexts, self-interest appears spontaneous and social concern effortful, whereas in others the reverse holds. This review argues that the inconsistency stems from a flawed premise. Drawing on converging evidence from social, affective, and decision neuroscience, I propose that both self-interest and social preferences are automatic motivational processes, driven by distinct motivational systems and regulated by separate prefrontal control mechanisms. The right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) is proposed to regulate reward-seeking motivation, facilitating prosocial behavior such as fairness and reciprocity, whereas the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (rVLPFC) is proposed to regulate socio-emotional responses, facilitating self-interested choice, together forming a proposed double dissociation within this motivational conflict. This dual-control framework reframes the central question from which motive is automatic to which automatic motivational system dominates a given context. It reconciles conflicting findings and explains why subtle situational shifts can reverse the apparent automatic response. The review considers emerging hormonal, neuromodulation, and hyperscanning evidence from dynamic interactions and discusses how changing circumstances may alter not only which motivation dominates, but also which form of control is needed to act in accordance with one's goals.

articles.title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. This suggests that achieving DEI goals in AI-integrated workplaces requires attention not only to the properties and behavior of AI, but also to employees' beliefs about AI itself.

articles.title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
articles.abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations.

articles.title: Your gain, my loss? Zero-sum thinking in negotiation
A meta-analysis of the dynamism of emergent states and team processes.
articles.abstract: Prevailing theories of teamwork propose that a team's cognitive, affective, and motivational states (i.e., emergent states) and its members' interdependent actions (i.e., team processes) are inherently dynamic. Nevertheless, much of the existing literature overlooks critical components of theories on system dynamics (e.g., inertia, coevolution, feedback) and has largely failed to consider how time operates, ultimately leading to a predominantly static view of teams. To extend our understanding of team dynamism, we synthesized over 3,000 correlation coefficients from longitudinal studies, representing more than 11,000 teams on average. Using cross-lagged, meta-analytic structural equation models, we found that (a) emergent states and team processes exhibit inertia over time, although this varies by construct (affect exhibits the least inertia, while conflict exhibits the most); (b) some constructs (team affect and team cognition) tend to coevolve with team processes over time, whereas others (team motivation and team conflict) are consistently predicted by earlier team processes; (c) team performance exhibits consistent feedback loops, predicting subsequent emergent states and processes, which, in turn, predict later performance; and (d) the length of time between observations moderates these dynamics. Drawing on these results, we outline several key theoretical considerations for understanding team dynamics, highlight important methodological considerations for conducting longitudinal causally identified teams research, and offer recommendations for advancing beyond the current static perspective to a more dynamic understanding of teams. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: A meta-analytic examination of the criterion-related validity and cognitive loading associated with traditional and new situational judgment test paradigms.
articles.abstract: Traditionally, situational judgment tests (SJTs) include text-based situations and ask candidates to pick the best and worst response option. Over the years, various new SJT paradigms have been developed to increase validity, reduce incidental cognitive load, and/or lower costs. Examples are multimedia SJTs, constructed response SJTs, and single-response SJTs. First, this study investigates how the traditional SJT paradigm performs in terms of criterion-related validity by updating prior meta-analyses. Second, this study provides initial, meta-analytic evidence on the criterion-related validity and cognitive load of several new SJT paradigms. On the basis of 457 independent samples from 302 studies (total N = 244,257), results showed that SJTs were not only predictive of job performance but also of academic performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and counterproductive work behavior. SJT validity was higher in operational (i.e., applicant) settings than in nonoperational settings and could also be expanded to new content (e.g., emotion and cross-cultural management). In terms of comparing traditional and new SJT paradigms, multimedia SJTs had validity equal to text-based ones but lower cognitive load. Importantly, the multiple-choice modality did not significantly outperform written constructed response modalities in terms of validity, and the cognitive loading of webcam-constructed responses was even lower than that of other response modalities. The implications of these findings are among others discussed in the context of the cost effectiveness of SJTs vis-à-vis other selection procedures. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Industrial-organizational science that matters: Social impact and policy implications in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
articles.abstract: This introductory article to the special issue "Social Impact Research" examines the extent to which research published in the Journal of Applied Psychology has addressed pressing social issues related to work and employment. Using BERTopic modeling on 5,865 empirical articles published from the journal's inception in 1917 through June 2024, we identified 99 topics organized into 25 higher order themes, five of which directly reflect social impact: workplace stress, health, and well-being; workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion; organizational justice, ethics, and legal issues; work and employment transitions across the lifespan; and social justice and labor opinions . Trend analyses from 1980 to 2024 revealed growth in health and well-being research, relatively stable publication of diversity, equity, and inclusion scholarship, an inverted-U trajectory for justice and legal topics, and the disappearance of labor-related research. We then introduce the 19 special issue articles (appearing in the October and November 2026 issues) which address employment barriers facing marginalized and economically disadvantaged workers, medical benefits and leave policies, gender and women's employment, and macrolevel societal disruptions, each offering actionable implications related to work that can benefit the greater good. We conclude by proposing a future social impact research agenda that suggests industrial-organizational (I-O) psychologists conduct research that addresses key issues such as economic insecurity, immigrant and refugee workers, generative artificial intelligence, climate change, and political instability. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: The shape of recovery activities: A person-centered study of evening recovery activity profiles, their work antecedents, and outcomes.
articles.abstract: Evening off-job activities play a crucial role in recovery from work. Although previous research has provided valuable insights into the role of recovery activities, little is known about the complex interplay of multiple characteristics of recovery activities and how this relates to well-being and work outcomes. Building on a dimensional approach to differentiate key characteristics of recovery activities (physical, social, creative, mental, spiritual, virtual, and outdoor), we adopt a person-centered perspective to identify distinct recovery activity profiles that capture the various ways these characteristics co-occur in daily life. We further investigate the extent to which these profiles shape recovery experiences, well-being, and work outcomes. Using data from two 10-day daily diary studies, Study 1 ( N = 345, 1,907 observations) identified daily profiles and demonstrated their associations with recovery experiences, emotional exhaustion, and next-morning vigor. In Study 2 ( N = 321, 1,780 observations), we assessed to what extent these profiles replicated in an independent sample and extended the investigation by including work-related antecedents and next-day work outcomes. Results indicated that daily recovery activities cluster together into identifiable profiles that largely replicated across samples. The identified profiles exhibited unique relationships with recovery experiences, well-being, and work outcomes. Our findings add to the recovery literature by illustrating the merits of considering profiles of recovery activities and their characteristics rather than studying recovery activities in isolation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: When the market moves: How stock market fluctuations shape risk-related behaviors at work.
articles.abstract: How employees' personal stock holdings perform during the day has become increasingly visible and accessible, yet research has rarely examined how fluctuations in those holdings shape employees' experiences at work. Integrating cross-domain spillover and regulatory focus theories, we propose that morning fluctuation in personal stock holdings spills over into the workplace by influencing employees' risk propensity-their willingness to take or avoid risks-and, in turn, their risk-related workplace behaviors. Specifically, drawing from regulatory focus theory, we propose that a more positive (vs. negative) fluctuation in personal stock holdings than usual is associated with subsequent increases (vs. decreases) in employees' willingness to engage in risk. In a 10-day experience sampling study of full-time employees who personally invest in the South Korean stock market, a more positive morning fluctuation in stock holding value than they typically experience predicted higher state risk propensity, which subsequently led to greater risk-taking behavior and voice. These indirect effects were moderated by long-term orientation, such that employees lower (vs. higher) in long-term orientation showed greater sensitivity to morning fluctuation in stock holding value. We then conducted two complementary experiments that supported the theorized regulatory focus mechanism by demonstrating that more positive fluctuation in personal stock holdings elicited promotion focus, whereas more negative fluctuation heightened prevention focus, and that these motivational states subsequently shaped employees' willingness to engage in risk. Together, these findings highlight employees' personal stock holdings as an overlooked source of daily behavioral variability at work. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Disentangling the effect of maternal mental health on children’s academic achievement: A random intercept approach.
articles.abstract: A wealth of transactional mother-child effects has been proposed in developmental research, including the potential influence of maternal mental health on children's academic development and vice versa. However, longitudinal multi-informant studies spanning several years remain scarce. In the present study, two birth cohorts were followed from ages 8 to 14 ( N = 747, 49.4% girls) to examine whether maternal anxiety and depression differentially predicted children's academic achievement and vice versa. A cross-lagged random-intercept model was applied to biennially collected data, controlling for stable, unmeasured, time-invariant factors (e.g., shared genetics, parental education) as well as time-varying covariates (e.g., negative life events). Results showed that higher levels of self-reported maternal anxiety and depression consistently predicted-at comparable magnitudes-lower teacher-reported academic achievement across all time points. These effects persisted after adjusting for prior levels of children's emotional problems, school performance, and exposure to negative life events. Moreover, lower academic achievement predicted increased maternal depressive symptoms between ages 10 and 12. The findings underscore the long-term impact of maternal mental health difficulties on children's functioning beyond the immediate family context, likely representing one of several mechanisms contributing to the intergenerational transmission of social marginalization. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Exploring gender beyond labels: Uncovering diverse gender groups with latent profile analysis.
articles.abstract: Gender is a variable of great interest to couples and family researchers who frequently use gender labels in individual, dyadic, and systems-level analyses. Labels are unsatisfactory representations of gender as a whole, as they may obfuscate nuanced gender experiences that impact health disparities for both transgender and cisgender respondents. However, there is a lack of consensus on how to model the multidimensionality of gender in quantitative analysis. The present study seeks to assess whether latent profile analysis can identify subgroups that could be used to observe patterns in disparities that would be unobserved by single-item gender measures. A sample of 2,404 U.S.-based respondents (79% White, 40% heterosexual, 20% gender minority) completed online surveys assessing the following indices: (a) sex assigned at birth, (b) degree of identification with binary labels (i.e., male and female), (c) expression/roles, and (d) fluidity. A parsimonious seven-group solution revealed four groups representing gender experiences aligned within a binary framework (strongly aligned masculine/feminine, moderately aligned masculine/feminine) and three groups representing experiences outside of the binary (aligned nonbinary feminine, aligned nonbinary/agender, aligned gender fluid). Cisgender and transgender participants appeared in each of the extracted gender classes, highlighting the limitations of gender labels for people across the gender spectrum. Health disparities also emerged across the gender groups, revealing unique challenges with regard to seeking counselling, microaggression exposure, internalized shame, depressive symptoms, and total lifetime suicide attempts. The results of this study provide a preliminary framework for integrating multiple dimensions into more inclusive subgroups. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Family interactions in youth at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P).
articles.abstract: This study examined family interactions in 162 youths at clinical high risk for psychosis and their mothers and fathers, using both observational data (a family problem-solving task) and self-report measures. We evaluated the association between family communication and youths' symptoms of psychosis, depression, and anxiety. Youths, mothers, and fathers rated family communication as one of the top three sources of family tension. During a 10-min problem-solving discussion, parents communicated significantly more constructively than clinical high risk for psychosis youths. Constructive communication was moderately correlated across parents and youth, suggesting reciprocity. There was moderate convergence between observed and self-reported communication. Mothers' constructive communication was positively associated with youths' unusual thoughts, perceptual abnormalities, and blunted affect and negatively associated with youths' depression. Youth with more internalizing symptoms perceived family communication more negatively. In line with attribution theory, mothers may respond more supportively to symptoms they see as uncontrollable and more critically to symptoms viewed as controllable. The sensitivities to social stimulation observed in many clinical high risk for psychosis youths, particularly those with negative symptoms and depression or anxiety, may contribute to feeling overwhelmed and aggravated by family interactions. Clinical implications of these findings are discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Identifying parent–sibling socialization profiles and their prospective associations with adolescents’ interpersonal competence.
articles.abstract: Family socialization plays a key role in adolescents' social development, yet little is known about how adolescents are socialized across different family subsystems beyond parental socialization. By using latent profile analysis to capture a holistic view of co-occurring family dynamics, this study aimed to identify different emotion socialization patterns in parent-adolescent and sibling subsystems and their longitudinal associations with adolescent interpersonal competence. Participants were 175 families with at least two children (target adolescent M age = 14.09, 47.4% female). At baseline (Time 1), caregivers reported emotion coaching and adolescents' sibling companionship and aggression; at 6-month follow-up (Time 2), adolescents reported interpersonal competence. Latent profile analysis was used to identify distinct profiles of family-level socialization at Time 1 and how adolescents' interpersonal competence differs across profiles at Time 2. A five-profile solution of parent-sibling socialization provided the best fit: low-support (4%), sibling-positive (29%), parent-positive (11%), overall-negative (29%), and overall-positive (27%). Significant differences emerged in all dimensions of interpersonal competence: Overall-positive adolescents reported higher scores of asserting influence, self-disclosure, and conflict resolution than all other profiles and higher scores of initializing relationships than those in all profiles except low-support. In addition, sibling-positive adolescents scored higher than overall-negative adolescents in providing emotional support and conflict resolution. Findings highlight the importance of concurrently considering multiple family subsystems, particularly the sibling subsystem, in socialization processes and their collective implications on adolescents' interpersonal competence. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Perceptions of relationship changes during pregnancy in Latinas: A qualitative study.
articles.abstract: Pregnancy is shaped by complex social dynamics and interpersonal changes that influence how expecting mothers connect with their families and others around them. While social support has been linked to better maternal mental health, less is known about how relationships themselves change during pregnancy. This study explores how pregnant Latinas living in the United States perceive changes in their family, partner, and peer relationships and how these evolving connections influence their sense of support. A subset of 48 pregnant Latinas who participated in a larger study took part in a one-on-one interview conducted in English or Spanish. Participants were recruited from community-based and institutional settings. Thematic analysis revealed three key themes and six subthemes. First, participants described strengthened maternal bonds with their own mothers and other close family members, along with increased relatability with other pregnant women. Second, participants often reported social withdrawal and isolation. This was driven by pregnancy symptoms, exclusion from social activities, and changes in how others treated them as a result of the pregnancy. Third, participants described varied changes in romantic relationship dynamics, including increased emotional distance for some, stability for others, and a desire for greater partner involvement. This study highlights the role of interpersonal relationships in shaping Latina's pregnancy experiences. Changes in family relationships, especially with maternal figures, as well as with partners and peers, influenced participants' emotional well-being and belonging during pregnancy. These findings highlight the need to consider relational dynamics in support efforts for Latinas and their families. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: The strain behind the smile: Temporal dynamics between parental burnout and emotional labor.
articles.abstract: Parents routinely engage in emotional labor to meet caregiving demands by faking emotions (surface acting) or by genuinely cultivating expected ones (deep acting). The association between emotional labor and parental burnout is an emerging question, yet predominantly cross-sectional evidence leaves directionality and temporal dynamics unclear. We therefore conducted two studies spanning different parent samples and timescales. Study 1 applied models from the cross-lagged panel family to a four-wave design with 4-month intervals among 1,373 U.S. parents of young adolescents. From an individual-differences perspective, surface acting and burnout were positively and reciprocally related, whereas the two emotional labor strategies were negatively so. From a within-person perspective, the only effect to emerge was that deep acting predicted lower subsequent surface acting. Study 2 applied dynamic structural equation modeling to a 35-day experience sampling design with 293 U.K. parents of younger children. Within parents, surface acting and burnout were positively and reciprocally related, burnout predicted more deep acting, and deep acting predicted less surface acting. Across parents, average levels during the experience sampling phase mediated baseline-to-follow-up associations for all constructs. We drew three conclusions. First, surface acting and parental burnout reinforce one another, whereas the effects of deep acting appear context-dependent. Second, timescale matters: Intensive longitudinal methods captured within-person processes that longer lagged panel designs missed. Third, patterns differed between our samples of parents of younger and older children, tentatively suggesting a developmental-stage influence; this finding needs confirmation before it can justify developmentally tailored family support. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Uncovering childcare struggles through topic modeling.
articles.abstract: Challenges with accessing reliable childcare are a main source of distress for many families with young children. Research has documented the detrimental effects of lack of access to stable and reliable care on caregivers and children, but little is known about which childcare-related challenges and impacts caregivers themselves perceive as most central. We bridge this gap by leveraging biterm topic modeling, a natural language processing technique, to analyze large-scale open-ended survey data, identify common themes brought up by parents when talking about childcare, and examine covariation with family characteristics. A six-topic solution was selected, clustered around two metatopics: access barriers and precarity experiences and psychosocial impacts of childcare challenges. Family characteristics, including child disability, identifying as female, identifying as Black, and having any higher education, were credibly associated with the likelihood of topic emergence in Bayesian regression models, with evidence varying in strength. Future work should focus on accurately measuring different dimensions of childcare challenges, as well as gauging causal and temporal relations between such challenges, family characteristics, and family outcomes. Policy and decision makers may use these and similar data to infer families' priorities when it comes to childcare. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Work-to-family conflict and family role performance among employed adult child caregivers: A moderated mediation model.
articles.abstract: Work-to-family conflict has significant implications for adult child caregivers and the older parents they care for, and cultural values such as filial piety play a critical role in shaping these dynamics. By integrating the work-home resources model with the dual filial piety framework, this study offers a novel perspective on how filial piety shapes the resource-depletion processes linking work-to-family conflict with family role performance. We conducted two empirical studies to test our hypotheses. Study 1 employed a time-lagged survey design and included 292 full-time employees who regularly provided care to their aging parents. Study 2 adopted a weekly experience sampling design, involving 256 participants and yielding 1,265 observations over a 5-week period. The results reveal that work-to-family conflict is negatively associated with family role performance. Informal caregiver burnout mediates this relationship. Moreover, reciprocal filial piety buffers the indirect effect of work-to-family conflict on family role performance through caregiver burnout, whereas authoritarian filial piety amplifies it. These findings highlight the role of culturally embedded filial norms in shaping resource dynamics and provide actionable insights for promoting caregiver well-being and eldercare quality in rapidly aging societies. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Linking Leader Overqualification to Employee Organizational Citizenship Behaviors Toward the Leader: A Personal Identification Process Model
articles.abstract: Overqualification has important implications not only for the overqualified but also those who work under the overqualified. Leaders are an influential source of self‐identity for followers and employee‐perceived leader overqualification impacts how followers view themselves and behave to the overqualified leader. Perceived leader overqualification, however, has both positive and negative impacts on followers. Yet, research on effects of follower perceived leader overqualification is limited. From an identification construction perspective, and drawing on personal identification (PI) process model, we theorize that perceiving a leader as overqualified can strengthen followers' identification with that leader and, in turn, their organizational citizenship behavior directed toward the leader (OCBL). Because identification depends on how followers construe a leader's attributes in relation to their own self‐concept, we position follower narcissism as a boundary condition. We argue that narcissistic admiration strengthens the positive link between perceived leader overqualification and leader identification, whereas narcissistic rivalry weakens it, producing divergent indirect effects on OCBL. Results from one vignette‐based experiment in the United States and two multi‐wave, multi‐source surveys in China consistently support this moderated‐mediation model. The findings reposition overqualification as a relationally consequential leader attribute and clarify when, and for whom, it elicits rather than undermines supportive follower behavior.

articles.title: When and Why Do Leaders Endorse Radical Ideas? A Transactional Theory of Stress Perspective
articles.abstract: Extant research has focused on the strategies that employees use to obtain leaders' endorsement of creative ideas that vary in radicalness, overlooking the possibility that these employee‐centric factors may backfire by increasing leaders' sense of threat. Drawing on the transactional theory of stress, we offer a leader‐centric perspective by identifying leader creative personality as a resource that influences when creative ideas with varying radicalness levels are more or less likely to be endorsed. We predict that (1) idea radicalness will exhibit a negative indirect relationship with endorsement through increased leader threat appraisal when leader creative personality is low, and (2) idea radicalness will have a positive indirect relationship with endorsement through increased leader challenge appraisal when leader creative personality is high. Results from a three‐wave field study of 167 leader–employee dyads showed that the indirect relationship between idea radicalness and endorsement was negative via increased leader threat appraisal when leader creative personality was low, and the indirect relationship was positive via decreased leader threat appraisal when leader creative personality was high. A scenario‐based experiment with 300 leader participants replicated the negative indirect relationship between idea radicalness and endorsement via leader threat appraisal when leader creative personality was low. Our findings suggest the importance of addressing leaders' threat appraisals of radical ideas, and we provide insights into how organizations can effectively leverage employees' radical ideas by managing leaders' sense of threat.

articles.title: Change perception at zero tolerance: How protected values bias sensitivity to social improvement.
articles.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
articles.abstract: Across six experiments, we examined how sensitivity to change varies with protected values (PVs). In Experiment 1, vegetarians were less appreciative than meat-eaters of large (but only partial) reductions in other people's meat consumption, but they were more appreciative than meat-eaters of smaller but absolute reductions (i.e., reduction to zero meat consumption). In Experiment 2, a similar pattern emerged in political groups: Republicans, who value immigration control more than Democrats, were relatively less sensitive to large but partial reductions in illegal immigration than to its elimination; the reverse pattern was observed for gun possession. In Experiment 3, we manipulated participants' values regarding child labor. Individuals who generated arguments in defense of child labor held less protected values and were comparatively more sensitive to change in child labor numbers. Further studies showed that protected values make people focus on the outcome (i.e., the present state) more than on the trajectory of change (i.e., the difference from the past; Experiment 4) and that they inspire stricter thresholds for what is considered acceptable (Experiment 5). Experiment 6 shows that protected values cause a heightened sensitivity to absolute changes to zero, rather than insensitivity to changes overall. These findings indicate that protected values amplify sensitivity to absolute changes to zero, compared to partial changes-even larger ones-that fall short of zero. The results have theoretical implications for theories of progress perception and quantity (in)sensitivity. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Contextual predictors of state loneliness: The role of social company, activity, location, and duration of contextual exposure.
articles.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
articles.abstract: Loneliness is not only a stable dispositional trait but also a momentary state that can fluctuate within individuals. However, empirical studies on how contextual factors relate to state loneliness remain scarce. This study investigated how state loneliness varies depending on social company, everyday activities, physical locations, and the duration of exposure to these contextual factors. Drawing on preregistered and exploratory analyses, we examined data from the Day Reconstruction Method module of the German Socio-Economic Panel Innovation Sample, collected across four waves between 2012 and 2015. The representative sample comprised 22,031 episodes nested within 2,508 participants (52.6% female, age range 17-95 years, M age = 50.0, SD age = 18.9). Multilevel logistic regression models showed that being alone consistently predicted higher odds of state loneliness, while the presence of others showed opposing associations. Participants were more likely to feel lonely when at home than when at work or elsewhere. Watching television was linked to a higher probability of reporting state loneliness, whereas self-care/health and media use showed a negative relationship. For some activities, this relationship was moderated by the duration of the activities: Reporting state loneliness was more likely during prolonged episodes of care work but less likely during prolonged episodes of social contact and television consumption. Overall, these findings contribute to a more robust, nuanced understanding of the contextual and temporal features tied to momentary feelings of loneliness, underscoring the need for dynamic, time-sensitive approaches in both research and interventions addressing everyday experiences of loneliness. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Shades of traits across languages: Comparisons of Dutch, Polish, Czech, and Serbian structures of behavioral items.
articles.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
articles.abstract: While trait adjectives may be regarded as convenient summary labels for varieties of behavioral expressions with common themes and outcomes, in turn, behaviors typical of a person may be considered as expressions of personality dispositions. In fact, in daily life, behavioral descriptions are way more frequent than the more abstract adjectival descriptors. For the present study, behavioral, verb-based data sets collected in four languages were used for comparison. The data sets each consisted of ratings from 400 participants on 543 Dutch personality verbs, 1,247 participants on 414 Polish personality verbs, 951 participants on 289 Czech personality verbs, and 512 participants on 319 Serbian personality verbs. Principal component analysis-based structures (of different dimensionalities) were compared pairwise across the languages, making use of congruence coefficients. Moreover, using simultaneous component analysis, the verb-based structure common to the four languages, based on a shared data set with ratings from 3,110 participants on 324 personality verbs, was analyzed. Three- and six-component structures based on the common set are discussed in some detail, both showing portions of the Big Five but with no reference to the Intellect-Imagination factor. It is concluded that verb-based behavioral items, in comparison to adjective- and noun-based items, give rise to a diluted and reduced trait-semantic space. To arrive at a full trait-semantic representation, all linguistic categories should be exploited in a joint operation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: The temporal dynamics of narcissism and aggression: Timescales, moderators, and generalizations in diverse samples.
articles.journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
articles.abstract: The relationship between narcissism and aggression has received considerable research attention, with the main conclusion being that individuals with higher levels of narcissism tend to exhibit more aggressive behavior. However, most evidence comes from cross-sectional and experimental studies using between-person analyses and relies heavily on Western convenience samples, leaving the temporal dynamics and within-person processes largely unexplored. This preregistered study examined four large-scale data sets of Chinese undergraduates and offenders: two ambulatory assessment samples (427 undergraduates and 775 offenders; 19,331 and 42,820 observations, respectively) and two long-term longitudinal samples ( N = 1,404, 969, 822, 613 for undergraduates and 2,064, 1,716, 1,609, 1,393 for offenders, each with four assessments over a year). Results indicated that narcissism and aggression prospectively predicted one another at the momentary level, but not the long-term level. These reciprocal effects were largely replicated across undergraduate and offender samples. Person-level narcissism and aggression moderated several of these dynamic associations, with the most robust pattern showing that higher person-level aggression consistently strengthened the effects of narcissistic states on subsequent aggression among offenders. Overall, this study provides, to our knowledge, the first within-person evidence for dynamic reciprocal associations between narcissism and aggression, while also offering stronger support for the robustness, cultural generalizability, and population representativeness of these processes. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

articles.title: Digital Masculinity and Digital Media Exposure in Relation to Male Genital Self-Image, Mental Health, and Sexual Health: A Scoping Review
articles.abstract: ABSTARCTMale genital self-image is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of men's sexual health, psychological well-being, and body image. The rapid expansion of social media, pornography, and digital masculinity ideals has raised concerns about their influence on unrealistic genital appearance expectations; however, evidence remains fragmented across disciplines. This scoping review mapped the literature on the relationships among digital masculinity, digital media exposure, male genital self-image, psychological well-being, and sexual health. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Electronic databases were systematically searched without publication year restrictions, and 27 studies met the eligibility criteria. Five major themes emerged: development and psychometric evaluation of male genital self-image measures, sociocultural and digital media influences, psychological correlates, sexual health outcomes, and penile dysmorphic concerns with related interventions. Overall, lower male genital self-image was associated with higher anxiety, depressive symptoms, social appearance anxiety, body dissatisfaction, and poorer sexual functioning. Social media, pornography, and masculinity norms appeared to reinforce unrealistic genital appearance ideals, although evidence regarding the direct effects of pornography remained inconsistent. Current evidence is dominated by cross-sectional studies from high-income countries, highlighting the need for longitudinal, cross-cultural, and intervention-based research to strengthen evidence and inform clinical practice.

articles.title: Dyadic Associations between Body Appreciation and Sexual Function among Cisgender Heterosexual and Gender and Sexually Diverse Couples
articles.abstract: Given the body's exposure during partnered sexual activity, having a positive perception of one's body may impact sexual function, i.e., the capacity to respond sexually. Yet research on the associations between body appreciation and sexual function within couples is limited, particularly among couples who identify as gender and sexually diverse, who face greater risks of experiencing sexual difficulties due to minority stress. Examining body appreciation among couples may lead to clearer insights into their sexual function. The present study assessed dyadic associations between body appreciation and sexual function, examining the moderating effects of gender identity and sexual orientation, in a diverse sample of 151 couples. Results based on the actor-partner interdependence moderation model showed that a person's body appreciation was negatively related to their own sexual function difficulties, and to their partner's difficulties when the latter was heterosexual. Gender identity did not significantly moderate these associations. This study demonstrates the associations between a person's body appreciation and their own sexual function, as well as the role of the partner's sexual orientation in the association between a person's body appreciation and their partner's sexual function, highlighting the importance of considering sexual orientation to understand dyadic associations with sexual health.

articles.title: Facilitators and Inhibitors of Healthy Sexuality Across the Life Course: A Qualitative Study of Sexual Trajectories, Reflection, and Agency
articles.abstract: Healthy sexuality has recently been proposed as a broader developmental framework that complements conventional concepts of sexual health. However, little empirical research has examined how healthy sexuality develops across the life course through lived experience. This study explores healthy sexuality by identifying facilitators and inhibitors of healthy sexuality and sexual satisfaction and by examining how they accumulate within individuals' sexual trajectories. Twenty semi-structured life-history interviews were conducted with participants aged 28-32 years in Slovakia. Data were analyzed using a combination of thematic analysis and narrative-phenomenological analysis. Facilitators and inhibitors were organized into four interrelated domains: intrapsychic, interaction with social norms, interpersonal, and physical. Paradoxical facilitators and inhibitors demonstrated that healthy sexuality and sexual satisfaction are not identical and may diverge under specific circumstances. Analysis of participants' sexual trajectories revealed three developmental pathways: (1) reflective development trajectories characterized by reflection, agency, and positive change; (2) reflective stagnation trajectories characterized by reflection without substantial behavioral change; (3) unreflective satisfaction trajectories characterized by apparent sexual satisfaction despite limited developmental potential for healthy sexuality. Findings support the conceptualization of healthy sexuality as a developmental process rather than a fixed state. The proposed framework may be inspirational for sexuality education, counseling, psychotherapy, and future research.

articles.title: Gender Minority Stress Experiences After Gender-Affirming Medical Care
articles.abstract: Understanding experiences of gender minority stress after gender-affirming medical care can improve post-treatment outcomes and provide transdiagnostic interventions targets for trans and gender diverse (TGD) individuals. This study aimed to describe proximal gender minority stress after gender-affirming care, and correlate high versus low stress to patient characteristics. In a cross-sectional study, participants were recruited through healthcare providers and community outlets to complete an online questionnaire. The quartiles with highest and lowest minority stress on the Transgender Identity Survey were included for analyses and compared on demographic and validated outcome questionnaires. Participants ( n = 86) frequently reported limited openness (42.4%) or support (19.7%) related to their TGD identity after medical treatments. Low proximal minority stress was associated with younger age, non-binary gender, moderate to full openness on TGD, and higher treatment satisfaction. Low minority stress was also associated with less anxiety/depression, higher self-esteem, social connectedness and life satisfaction (moderate to large effect sizes). Open-text answers suggested that minority stress experiences were heterogeneous and related to persistent gender-based distress, stressful social interactions, and/or negative treatment outcomes. Minority stress theory can provide a transdiagnostic concept to improve the wellbeing of TGD individuals after medical transition, while substantial conceptual overlap with mental health outcomes exists.

articles.title: Marital Adjustment, Parenting Stress, and Gender Role Attitudes Among Married Individuals: An Actor–Partner Interdependence Analysis*
articles.abstract: Marriage and parenting are relational experiences shaped by mutual interactions between partners; however, most studies have examined these processes at the individual level. This cross-sectional correlational study investigated actor and partner associations among gender role attitudes, parenting stress, and marital adjustment in 153 married heterosexual couples in Türkiye using the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model. Data were collected using the Gender Roles Attitude Scale, Parenting Stress Scale, and Marital Adjustment Scale. More egalitarian gender role attitudes were associated with lower parenting stress and higher marital adjustment at the actor level in both women and men. Parenting stress was not significantly associated with individuals' own marital adjustment. Partner effects showed gendered patterns: men's egalitarian gender role attitudes were positively associated with women's marital adjustment, whereas women's gender role attitudes were not significantly associated with men's marital adjustment. In addition, parenting stress showed significant crossover associations, with men's parenting stress showing a numerically larger standardized association with women's marital adjustment than the reverse pathway. These findings highlight the interdependent nature of couple relationships and suggest that gender role attitudes and parenting stress may operate not only within individuals but also across partners in relation to marital adjustment.

articles.title: Moving Beyond a Binary Cis-Heteronormative Perspective: A Scoping Review of Instruments for Inclusive Research into Sexual Functioning
articles.abstract: Cis- and heteronormativity hinder the valid measurement of sexual function in Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity (SOGD) populations. This study aimed to identify instruments designed for inclusive use and to evaluate their cross-cultural and psychometric characteristics. A scoping review was conducted by searching PubMed, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science in April 2026. The search terms included sexual function, gender, sexual orientation, assessment instruments, and psychometric information. Screening, data extraction, and quality grading were performed independently by two reviewers. Fifteen articles described the development or validation of instruments for use among SOGD populations. Notably, non-binary individuals were included in only one study. For most instruments, adequate content and structural validity, and internal consistency were reported, but evidence for cross-gender, cross-sexual orientation, cross-cultural, criterion, and construct validity was lacking or unclear. Limited or no information was provided on test-retest reliability, measurement error, and responsiveness to changes in sexual function for the instruments used. Most identified instruments were validated in narrowly defined subgroups or assessed only a single domain of sexual functioning, limiting their suitability as general, SOGD-inclusive measures. This review supports the need to develop and validate new inclusive instruments to measure sexual function, including SOGD populations.

articles.title: Sexual Distress, Concerns About Sex Life, and Successful Sexual Aging: An Exploration in Older Partnered German Adults
articles.abstract: Although research on older adults' sexual functioning and sexual health has increased in recent decades, there is a lack of systematic assessments of the role of sexual distress in positive sexual aging. This study examined associations between sexual distress, concerns about sex life, and positive sexual aging, and whether these associations differ by gender. Data were drawn from a 2024 online survey of partnered, sexually active German adults aged 65 years and older ( n = 598). Positive sexual aging was assessed using the Successful Sexual Aging Scale (SSAS). Structural equation modeling controlling for age showed that distress about sexual functioning was strongly and negatively associated with successful sexual aging in both women and men. Concerns about sex life were additionally and uniquely associated with lower SSAS scores among women. Findings underscore the importance of assessing sexual distress and gender-specific concerns in older adults' sexual health care.

articles.title: Sexual Quality of Life After Feminizing Genital Gender-Affirming Surgery in Transgender Women: Associations with Psychological Resilience and Body Image
articles.abstract: Sexual quality of life after feminizing genital gender-affirming surgery remains insufficiently characterized, particularly regarding psychosocial factors. This single-center retrospective cross-sectional survey examined associations of body image and psychological resilience with sexual quality of life in 39 transgender women after feminizing genital gender-affirming surgery, all sexually active in the preceding month. Sexual quality of life, psychological resilience, and body image were assessed using validated Turkish self-report instruments. Bivariate associations were examined using Spearman correlations, and exploratory ordinary least-squares regression examined the associations of psychological resilience and body image with sexual quality of life; age and postoperative duration were also explored. Psychological resilience was strongly correlated with sexual quality of life (rₛ = 0.900) and body image (rₛ = 0.864), and body image with sexual quality of life (rₛ = 0.764; all p < 0.001). Neither age nor postoperative duration was significantly associated with any measure. Psychological resilience and body image were each strongly associated with postoperative sexual quality of life and were themselves closely interrelated. These findings support considering psychosocial factors within a broader multidimensional assessment of postoperative sexual well-being.

articles.title: The Effect of Sexual Counseling with the PLISSIT Model on Sexual Function and Sexual Quality of Life in Women with Multiple Sclerosis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.abstract: Sexual dysfunction is common in women with MS, but evidence on long-term effects of PLISSIT counseling is limited. This randomized trial evaluated its 12-month effects on sexual function and quality of life. Eighty-six women aged 18-45 years were randomized to counseling (n = 43) or control (n = 43). Sixty-three participants completed all follow-up assessments and were included in the complete-case analysis (counseling, n = 31; control, n = 32). The intervention comprised four counseling sessions over four weeks. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and 3, 6, and 12 months using the Multiple Sclerosis Intimacy and Sexuality Questionnaire-15 (MSISQ-15), Sexual Quality of Life Questionnaire-Female (SQOL-F), and self-reported weekly intercourse frequency. Significant group × time interactions occurred for MSISQ-15 total (p = 0.006), primary sexual dysfunction (p = 0.029), and secondary sexual dysfunction (p 0.05). SQOL-F and intercourse frequency showed significant time effects (both p < 0.001). SQOL-F improved from baseline to 6 months and from 6 to 12 months (both p < 0.001). Intercourse frequency was higher with counseling at 6 (p < 0.001) and 12 months (p = 0.004). PLISSIT-based counseling was associated with different longitudinal patterns and greater sexual activity; however, improvements in sexual quality of life cannot be attributed solely to the intervention.

articles.title: “It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb”: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives
articles.abstract: This study examines how this generation of young heterosexual men-who have come of age in the "age of consent"-emotionally experience sex. We thematically analyzed 31 in-depth interviews with men aged 18 to 32 years. The most striking finding is how rarely these men described enjoying sex. Three themes emerged. First, anxiety and vigilance accompanied sexual encounters. Second, there was a moral concern about causing harm to a sexual partner. Third, shame arose not only from accusations by others, but also from self-criticism. The themes overlap substantially, suggesting aspects of a complex, sometimes contradictory experience. The defining feature is an inward turn: a cultural suspicion of men appears to have been internalized by some young men. For these men, the question when navigating consent is often not only "does she want this?" but "am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?" Sex, as one participant put it, is "like you're trying to defuse a bomb." These young men have come to approach sex as a hazard to manage rather than a relational experience to share. They attributed this wariness to the cultural climate that surrounds consent. We consider implications for consent education, clinical practice, and future research.

articles.title: Beyond Asexuality as a Single Category: Sexuality-Related Profiles and Differential Perceived Stigma-Related Impairment Across the Ace Spectrum
articles.abstract: Asexuality is increasingly understood as a heterogeneous spectrum, yet research has rarely examined how multiple sexuality-related dimensions cluster within ace-spectrum (i.e. asexual-spectrum) populations or how such configurations relate to perceived stigma-related impairment. Using data from the 2021 Ace Community Survey (analytic N = 11,063), this study adopted a multidimensional, person-centered approach to identify sexuality-related profiles based on sexual attraction frequency, desire to act on attraction, sex drive/libido, and sex disposition. Latent profile analysis (LPA) identified four profiles: Sex-Averse Low-Attraction, Context-Dependent Low-Attraction, Higher-Frequency, and Sex-Favorable High-Attraction. The Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars approach was used to compare these profiles on a global index of perceived asexuality-related impairment and four domain-specific outcomes: harm to family relationships, socioeconomic disadvantage, social exclusion, and mental/physical health impairment. Although overall impairment levels were low, the Higher-Frequency profile showed comparatively greater perceived impairment across domains. The Sex-Averse Low-Attraction and Sex-Favorable High-Attraction profiles generally showed lower perceived impairment and did not differ from each other, except for socioeconomic disadvantage, for which the Sex-Favorable High-Attraction profile showed comparatively elevated scores. The Context-Dependent Low-Attraction profile typically fell between these groups. These findings indicate that ace-spectrum sexuality is internally heterogeneous and that sexuality-related configurations are associated with distinct patterns of perceived stigma-related impairment. By documenting within-spectrum differences, this study advances a more differentiated understanding of asexuality, minority stress, and sexuality-related vulnerability.

articles.title: In Harm’s Way: How the 2024 U.S. Election Might Affect Sexual- and Gender-Minority Health
articles.abstract: Immediately after taking office in 2025, the current U.S. presidential administration established an unprecedented number of policies hostile to sexual- and gender-minority (SGM) populations: restricting the rights and social legitimacy of transgender individuals, curtailing youth access to gender-affirming medical care, terminating federal research and data collection on sexual and gender diversity, and restricting open discussion of sexual and gender diversity in educational settings. These events pose a greater threat to SGM health than previous state-level hostile policies, because of their scope, speed, and scale, and because they serve to institutionalize animus toward gender-minority populations into U.S. law and policy. We use extant research on structural stigma to predict the most likely mental and physical health consequences of these events, and we also forecast health consequences for the family members of SGM individuals and individuals whose paid employment involves SGM populations. We review evidence for the mechanisms through which these effects may unfold (institutional changes, increased minority stress, decreased social safety, and behavioral changes) and identify subpopulations at disproportionate risk (gender-minority populations, youth, those facing intersectional stigma, and those with existing health vulnerabilities). We conclude with a call for targeted efforts to ameliorate these negative health consequences, and we review research indicating that increasing social support and safety is the most effective and feasible strategy for doing so. We call for urgent, community-based efforts to increase the number and quality of nurturant social connections among all individuals who have been placed in harm's way by the changed U.S. political climate.

articles.title: Measuring Automatic Cognitive Responses to Erotic Stimuli Using Implicit Association Tests: Reliability and Validity Aspects
articles.abstract: Recently, implicit associations have been forwarded as relevant cognitive determinants of sexual desire and arousal. In the present study, using a cross-sectional design, implicit association tests (IAT) were used to measure the strength of automatic associations of erotic stimuli with positive versus negative valence (liking IAT) and with wanting versus not wanting (wanting IAT). The internal consistency and temporal stability, and the construct and criterion validity of the IATs were investigated. Additionally, the effects of stimulus mode on the psychometric properties of these IATs were examined. For this purpose, picture-and-word and full-picture IAT versions of the liking and wanting IATs were compared. Sexual function was measured using the Female Sexual Function Index for women and the International Index of Erectile Function for men. To examine the construct and criterion validity of the IATs, the Sexual Opinion Survey (SOS) and the Sexual Thoughts Questionnaire (STQ) were administered. A community sample was examined ( N = 335 total; 234 women). The internal consistency and temporal stability of all IATs were found satisfactory to excellent. The criterion validity of the IATs demonstrated only a few small-size correlations with explicit sexual attitudes. Contrary to similar previous research, the IATs did not predict sexual function level. Speculative explanations for these unexpected findings are presented.

articles.title: Mediators and Moderators of Treatment Outcome Following Online Mindfulness and Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment for Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder
articles.abstract: eSense is a digital tool delivering mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to individuals with female sexual interest/arousal disorder (SIAD). eSense is feasible, usable, satisfying, and efficacious, and helps overcome barriers to care. We sought to examine potential mediators and moderators of improvements in sexual desire and distress following use of eSense . Women with SIAD ( n = 129, mean age 44.8 ± 12.3 in the MBT arm and 41.9 ± 13.1 in the CBT arm) were randomly assigned to arm and completed self-report measures at baseline, mid-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and 6-month follow-up. Potential mediators were changes in depression, posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms (PTSD), and avoidance of sexual activity. We examined treatment expectations after module 1 as a potential moderator, and partner involvement, homework completion, and modules completed as process indicators that may predict magnitude of improvement. Decreases in depressive and PTSD symptoms were associated with improvements in sexual desire and distress in the MBT arm, and reductions in sexual avoidance were associated with improvements in both arms. Higher expectations for treatment were associated with greater improvements in desire and distress for those in the CBT arm only, whereas partner involvement, homework completion, and number of eSense modules completed were associated with improvements in both arms. This study helps identify putative mechanisms by which digital health tools for SIAD, like eSense , may be effective, and to identify participant characteristics as well as treatment engagement factors that might be associated with differential responses to online MBT and CBT.

articles.title: Predictors of Sexual Aggression Intentions Among Sexual Minority Men: Exploring the Utility of Vignette Methodologies
articles.abstract: Sexual violence (SV) is prevalent yet understudied among sexual minority men (SMM), leaving gaps in understanding perpetration risk. Experimental analogues are commonly used to examine SV perpetration among heterosexual samples, yet little to no research has examined whether these methods are relevant to SMM, limiting researchers' ability to identify unique predictors among this population. This study examined the feasibility of using vignette methodologies with SMM and investigated empirically supported predictors of aggressive sexual intentions. First, among the full sample ( N = 604), we assessed the feasibility and validity of using written SV vignettes with SMM ( n = 253) by comparing their perceptions of scenario realism, immersion, and sexual arousal to those of heterosexual men ( n = 351). SMM rated the vignettes as similarly realistic and engaging, supporting their utility for this population. Second, limiting the analytic sample to SMM, we tested a model in which internalized homophobia predicted sexually aggressive intentions via male rape myth acceptance (MRMA), conditional on self-reported sexual interest and perceived partner interest. These findings highlight the importance of addressing MRMA and situational misperceptions in prevention efforts. Tailored interventions that consider both internalized stigma and contextual risk factors are critical for reducing SV perpetration risk among SMM.

articles.title: Turning the Lens on Sexual Perpetration: Predictors of Acknowledging Sexual Perpetration
articles.abstract: Factors related to sexual perpetration acknowledgment are virtually unstudied, leaving a significant gap in the sexual violence literature. The current study explored (1) perpetration frequency and tactics and (2) acceptance of myths about sexual aggression (AMASA) as potential predictors of acknowledgment. In addition, post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms were examined as possible correlates of perpetration acknowledgment. A secondary aim of this study was to provide descriptive data for the proportion of people who have sexually perpetrated and who also endorse being victimized (i.e. victim-perpetrator overlap in adulthood) as well as rates of perpetration acknowledgment in this sample. The data used were from a larger study of 1,177 participants recruited from Prolific, a university research pool, and snowball methods using a cross-sectional design. Of the 722 eligible participants, 305 (42.2%) endorsed perpetration and 302 (99.0%) of those endorsed victim-perpetrator overlap. Our results revealed positive associations between frequency and acknowledgment. Further, there were significant differences between the tactic used and acknowledgment. Finally, group differences based on acknowledgment were found when examining AMASA and psychological distress. The current study addressed critical gaps in the literature by examining factors related to perpetration acknowledgment, providing insights that can guide future research, develop theory, and inform interventions.

articles.title: Use of Post-Coital Strategies to Prevent Pregnancy: Findings from a National Sample of Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States
articles.abstract: In the context of increasing restrictions on sexual and reproductive health care, inadequate sex education, and increasing antihormonal contraceptive sentiment, we examined post-coital pregnancy prevention behavior among a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents and young adults (AYA). We developed a novel measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies (i.e., actions taken after sexual intercourse with the intent of reducing the likelihood of pregnancy) and fielded this measure for the first time as part of a 2025 online, population-based survey of English-speaking 15-29-year-olds assigned female at birth ( n = 1,259). Of the 633 AYA who reported having ever had penile-vaginal sex and were not currently pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy to prevent pregnancy the last time they had sex. While methods with established effectiveness (i.e., emergency contraception and copper intrauterine device) were used by 8.9% respondents, 16.1% reported using a non-medically evidenced post-coital strategy, the most common being praying (9.4%). Post-coital strategy use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods used. In multivariable analyses, contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with post-coital strategy use. Regardless of effectiveness, post-coital strategies are common enough to warrant inclusion in behavioral surveillance and attention in health education and clinical practice.

articles.title: Associations Between Adult Attachment and Social Anxiety in Romantic Partner Situations: Does Perceived Dyadic Coping Play a Mediational Role?
articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
articles.abstract: Adult attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are associated with negative individual and relational outcomes. However, it is unknown whether these insecure attachment styles are associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations, and whether dyadic coping may play a mediating role in these associations. The current study tested these possibilities. A community sample of adults who reported being in a romantic relationship ( N = 88) completed measures of adult attachment, dyadic coping style of their partner, and a newly developed measure of social anxiety for romantic partner situations. Attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were significantly and positively associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations. Perceived negative dyadic coping partially mediated these associations, whereas perceived supportive dyadic coping did not mediate these associations. These findings suggest that an individual’s insecure attachment style is associated with higher social anxiety levels in relation to their romantic partner, and this association is in part accounted for by the perception of negative dyadic coping of the partner in response to stressors within the relationship. The findings also highlight the importance of relationship-based mediators in explaining links between insecure adult attachment styles and their outcomes.

articles.title: Lonely in Love, Driven to Buy: How Perceived Partner Materialism Influences Loneliness and Consumption in Romantic Relationships
articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
articles.abstract: Loneliness is increasingly prevalent and carries significant consequences for well-being, yet it remains common even within romantic relationships. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory and the Discrepancy Model of Loneliness, this research conceptualizes loneliness as arising when relationships fail to satisfy individuals’ need for relatedness, resulting in perceived gaps in closeness. Moving beyond prior work on value congruence, this research examines how perceptions of a partner’s materialism are associated with loneliness, relational outcomes, and consumption behavior. Results from a survey study ( N = 546) indicate that both perceived partner materialism and personal materialism are associated with greater loneliness, suggesting that unmet expectations for closeness, not value similarity, are linked to this experience. In contrast, perceived partner materialism is related to higher relationship satisfaction only among individuals who are themselves more materialistic. Perceived partner materialism and loneliness are also associated with compulsive buying and product retention tendency, even after controlling for personal materialism. Together, the findings highlight the role of perceived partner values in shaping both relationship experiences and consumer responses to unmet relational needs.

articles.title: Patterns in Mother-Child and Father-Child Mutually Responsive Orientation During Mealtimes: Correlation With Martial Satisfaction
articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
articles.abstract: Marital relationship and parent-child interaction have been found to be correlated. Using observational data from family mealtime interactions, this study examined mother-child and father-child mutually responsive orientation (MRO) among toddlers (18-24 months) during mealtime and its association with mother-reported marital satisfaction. MRO refers to a positive, reciprocal, and cooperative parent–child relationship that serves as a foundation for early socialization. Our final sample consisted of 71 families. Latent profile analysis identified a four-class solution. Class 1 reflected moderately high interaction quality for both father–child and mother–child relationships. Class 2 was characterized by moderate father–child interaction quality coupled with low mother–child interaction quality. Class 3 demonstrated comparatively lower father–child interaction quality and high mother–child interaction quality. Finally, Class 4 represented high-quality interactions for both fathers and mothers across domains. Findings further indicated that families characterized by lower-quality father–child interactions alongside higher-quality mother–child interactions reported the lowest levels of maternal marital satisfaction. In contrast, when fathers demonstrated moderate or high-quality interactions with their child, mothers reported higher marital satisfaction, regardless of the quality of mother–child interactions. These results underscore the importance of father–child interaction quality in shaping mothers’ perceptions of marital satisfaction.

articles.title: Self-Esteem as a Shared Resource Beyond Romantic Relationships: An Extension Into Friendships and Parental Relationships
articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
articles.abstract: Self-esteem is an important factor in understanding relationship quality, for both the individual and their romantic partner. Yet, most research has focused on solely romantic relationships, neglecting other close relationships that are at least equally important for understanding humans. In the present analysis, introductory psychology students at a Canadian university and their significant other (romantic partner, close friend, or primary caregiver) completed measures of self-esteem and relationship quality ( N = 308 dyads). Actor-Partner Interdependence Model analyses replicated and extended Robinson and Cameron’s (2012) findings that the higher dyad members’ combined self-esteem, the higher the dyad-level relationship quality. Thus, self-esteem may serve as a shared resource in romantic, friend, and family relationships.

articles.title: Which Way Does Cupid’s Arrow Go? Distinguishing Happiness and Meaningfulness Within Romantic Relationships
articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
articles.abstract: Happiness and meaningfulness are viewed as distinct aspects of psychological wellbeing, but their role in romantic relationships remains unknown. In two online studies, we sought to identify key differences between people’s judgments of relationship happiness and meaningfulness. Study 1 ( n = 426) found that greater sexual desire and satisfaction, and fewer relationship sacrifices and less stress, contributed to relationship happiness but were unconnected to relationship meaningfulness. By contrast, greater negative self-disclosure to one’s partner predicted relationship meaningfulness but was unlinked to relationship happiness. Study 2 ( n = 711) successfully replicated these findings, and further showed that people who prefer a meaningful relationship (over a happy one) exhibit a more favorable psychosocial profile, including greater relationship satisfaction, optimism, interpersonal closeness, forgiveness, and less relationship stress. These studies are the first to show that a distinct profile of psychosocial correlates distinguishes happy from meaningful romantic relationships, and they highlight the need for future research to consider hedonic and eudaimonic elements in relationship processes separately.

articles.title: Are the basic psychological needs of self-determination theory necessary for employee well-being?
articles.abstract: The basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness in self-determination theory (SDT) were originally defined and interpreted as necessary for well-being. Although this necessity assumption has been a cornerstone of SDT for over three decades, no systematic evidence has yet emerged to support it. This knowledge gap largely stems from a theory-method misfit. Most empirical studies use regression-based analytical techniques that do not align with necessity logic because they reflect a probabilistic “average-effect” logic. Necessary condition analysis (NCA) is an appropriate method specifically designed for identifying necessary conditions. In the present research, we adopt NCA to examine whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness are necessary for employee evaluative well-being (job satisfaction and work meaningfulness), affective well-being (positive affect), and conative well-being (work engagement). Across three studies, we found consistent support for the necessary role of psychological need satisfaction in all four well-being indicators, with nuanced variations in these necessity relationships. In contrast, power and status were not found to be necessary. These findings advance our understanding of basic psychological needs through a necessity-oriented lens and underscore the importance of fostering a need-supportive work environment in organizations.

articles.title: Daily job crafting with generative artificial intelligence: Implications for work meaningfulness and engagement
articles.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) becomes embedded in daily work, understanding how employees proactively engage with these tools to shape their work experiences is increasingly important. Building on self-determination theory and the job crafting literature, this study introduces the concept of daily Gen-AI-driven job crafting: employees' self-initiated use of Gen-AI to modify their daily job demands and resources. We examine whether Gen-AI-driven job crafting is associated with daily work engagement through psychological need satisfaction and work meaningfulness. We employed a daily diary design with 149 UK-based full-time employees (M age = 36.7, SD age = 10.4; 63.8% male) who used Gen-AI at work daily or multiple times per day over ten consecutive workdays, incorporating a brief open-ended question to examine whether employees experienced their Gen-AI use as intentional work modification. Quantitative results showed that the dimensions of Gen-AI-driven job crafting (augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands) were differentially associated with daily work engagement through need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and, in turn, work meaningfulness: the competence pathway received the most consistent support, while the relatedness pathway was the most limited. Open-ended responses were consistent with intentional work modification, for instance, automating hindering demands was framed as a strategic reallocation of cognitive resources toward more valued work rather than simple workload reduction. Together, these findings suggest that Gen-AI may function as a bottom-up work design tool associated with daily need satisfaction and engagement.

articles.title: Decoding fairness: Unveiling the cognitive processes that determine pay rises and promotions
articles.abstract: Drawing on attribution theory, this study explores how employees explain organizational decisions concerning pay rises and promotions, conceptualizing these attributional processes as an interpretive layer that precedes fairness evaluations, and how distinct configurations of causal explanations are associated with work-related attitudes. The research was conducted in an Italian bank, leveraging on a two-wave design and a two-study structure. The full sample ( N = 3193) was randomly split into two equivalent subsamples.
